query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored slow-cooling post-solution annealing treatment will induce serrated grain boundaries in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 HEA, enhancing its load-bearing integrity while preserving its caloric performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with conventional, relatively straight grain boundaries
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a solution-treatment (e.g., 900 °C for 60 minutes) followed by a controlled slow-cooling process at ~1 °C/min to room temperature
generation.conditions: Applied fields: magnetic field and pressure conditions identical to operational refrigeration regimes; temperature operating range from ambient to near the caloric transition temperature; standard tensile loading rates for integrity tests
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of serrated grain boundaries with coarser, evenly distributed intergranular precipitates
generation.mechanism: Serrated boundaries distribute local stresses more evenly, reducing stress concentration sites and arresting microcrack propagation, while the bulk phase transformation responsible for the caloric effect remains unaltered
generation.predicted_outcome: Fracture toughness and load-bearing capacity increase by an estimated 20–50% over baseline, with the caloric (field/pressure-induced) entropy change reduced by less than 10% compared to the untreated alloy
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits large caloric responses but suffers from premature cracking under load
generation.boundary: Operable under magnetic field strengths and pressures as previously used; temperature cycling within 20–100 °C; tensile stresses as per standard mechanical testing (e.g., strain rate ~10^−3 s^−1)
generation.uncertainty: Potential alterations to the kinetics of the caloric phase transformation or inadvertent coarsening of the functional phase if the cooling rate is not optimized

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one set processed via the controlled slow-cooling treatment and one set as-cast. Characterize the grain boundary morphology using SEM/TEM and measure mechanical properties (fracture toughness, tensile strength) as well as caloric performance (e.g., magnetocaloric or barocaloric entropy change).
measurements: Grain boundary morphology (serration amplitude and wavelength)
Fracture toughness and tensile strength tests
Caloric effect evaluation (entropy change, hysteresis) under applied fields/pressure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated alloy does not show at least a 20% improvement in fracture toughness and load-bearing capacity, or if its caloric performance degrades by more than 10% relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. This work has demonstrated that a simple post heat treatment could induce SEGB in a HEA fabricated by SLM. The serrations on grain boundary in HT-samples were attributed to the blocky irregular shaped γ′ precipitates formed during the slow cooling process, and they could pin the mobile grain boundaries as well as restricting grain growth, this phenomenon is known as the Zener drag effect []. The drag force from the coarse precipitates would hinder the migration of grain boundary, while those free from the precipitates could break free around the precipitates and resulted in serrated morphology (Figure 4(c)). The inhibition of grain growth from coarse precipitates explained why HT-2 sample possessed a smaller grain size than that of HT-1 sample. papers.title: Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing.
papers.approach: Cryo-rolling to 90% reduction in thickness followed by annealing at 800 °C
papers.findings: The processed alloy developed a hierarchical, heterogeneous microstructure featuring ultrafine recrystallized lamellae interspersed with coarser regions. This resulted in a marked increase in yield and ultimate tensile strength while maintaining good ductility relative to the as-cast state.
papers.mechanism: The combination of severe plastic deformation via cryo-rolling and subsequent annealing induces partial recrystallization and nano-lamellar structures that act as internal constraints, thereby providing a synergistic enhancement of strength and ductility.

papers.title: Heterogeneous precipitation mediated heterogeneous nanostructure enhances strength-ductility synergy in severely cryo-rolled and annealed CoCrFeNi₂.₁Nb₀.₂ HEA
papers.approach: Severe cryo-rolling (90% thickness reduction) combined with annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour
papers.findings: Compared to its cold-rolled counterpart, the cryo-rolled and annealed alloy formed a heterogeneous microstructure with retained deformed regions and ultrafine recrystallized zones. This microstructure led to excellent strength–ductility synergy.
papers.mechanism: Accelerated precipitation of nanoscale ε-phase during annealing in the cryo-rolled alloy inhibited complete recrystallization, resulting in a microstructure that combines both deformed and recrystallized regions which together enhance load-bearing capacity.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Al₈Co₃₅Cr₁₈Ni₃₄Ti₃Nb₂Zr₀.₀₀₅B₀.₀₁ (at.%) high-entropy alloy fabricated by selective laser melting
papers.approach: Post solution heat treatment with a reduced cooling rate to promote grain boundary serration through coarsening of γ′ precipitates
papers.findings: The introduction of serrated grain boundaries improved the tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life significantly relative to alloys with straight grain boundaries, by distributing strain more evenly and reducing stress concentrations at triple junctions.
papers.mechanism: The slow cooling facilitates the coarsening of second-phase precipitates that interact with migrating grain boundaries (via Zener drag), thereby generating a serrated morphological profile. This morphology helps arrest microcrack propagation and better distribute local strains under load.

established: Thermomechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling and annealing) of HEAs can produce hierarchical microstructures that significantly improve strength and ductility.

Grain boundary morphology, particularly transitioning from straight to serrated boundaries via controlled cooling, is effective in reducing local strain concentrations, enhancing ductility and delay crack propagation.

approaches_tried.approach: Severe plastic deformation (cryo-rolling) with subsequent annealing
approaches_tried.outcome: Remarkable increase in strength without substantial loss of ductility by inducing heterogeneous, nanolamellar microstructures.

approaches_tried.approach: Post heat treatment with slow cooling to induce serrated grain boundaries
approaches_tried.outcome: Increased tensile fracture strain and extended creep rupture life, with strain more evenly distributed at the boundaries.

mechanisms: Hierarchical microstructural constraint from combined ultrafine grains and heterogeneous regions enhances strength and ductility.
Serrated grain boundaries reduce stress concentrations by pinning local dislocation motion and arresting microcrack propagation.
Zener drag from coarsened second-phase precipitates interacting with grain boundaries induces beneficial morphological undulations.
disagreements: While some studies report that extreme processing (e.g., severe rolling) may degrade ductility through excessive fragmentation, others achieve simultaneous strength and ductility via controlled heat treatment.
There is some uncertainty in the prediction of phase evolution (e.g., the presence of certain precipitates) where simulation and experimental observations diverge.
open_questions: Can a controlled post-synthesis heat treatment intervention that targets grain boundary serration improve load-bearing integrity in caloric HEAs without impairing their caloric (field/pressure-driven) response?
How will the modified microstructure interact with the underlying phase transformation processes responsible for the caloric effect?
What are the boundaries for processing conditions (temperature, cooling rate) that preserve the functional caloric performance while enhancing mechanical integrity?
opportunities: Apply a tailored slow-cooling heat treatment post-fabrication to induce serrated grain boundaries in the (MnNiSi)₀.₆₂(FeCoGe)₀.₃₈ alloy.
Combine the benefits of microstructural heterogeneity (from prior cryo-rolling studies) with grain boundary engineering to achieve both improved integrity and maintained caloric performance.

Conduct systematic investigations to map the influence of cooling rate and temperature on both the caloric properties and mechanical load-bearing capacity, an approach not yet reported for these caloric high-entropy refrigerants.

directions.direction: Tailored slow‐cooling heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries
directions.assessment: Directly targets intergranular cracking by modifying grain boundary morphology. Prior work (e.g., PMC9848264) shows serrated grain boundaries can markedly reduce stress concentrations without impairing functional properties. Feasible and well‐supported by known mechanisms.

directions.direction: Trace microalloying (e.g., small Zr addition) to promote fine, coherent grain‐boundary precipitates
directions.assessment: A minor compositional tweak can lead to precipitation of secondary phases along boundaries that improve toughness. Evidence (e.g., PMC8539796) suggests Zr‐modification can lower melting temperature with coherent precipitates; however, care is needed to preserve the field‐induced caloric transformation.

directions.direction: Low-strain friction stir processing to refine the grain structure and create a more homogeneous microstructure
directions.assessment: FSP can reduce porosity and refine grains, which enhances load-bearing capacity. Although promising from a mechanical integrity perspective, its impact on caloric phase transitions is less documented.

directions.direction: Two‐step post‐synthesis annealing: a high-temperature homogenization followed by a slow-cooling step
directions.assessment: This combined treatment aims to first homogenize the alloy and then, via controlled slow cooling, develop beneficial grain‐boundary features while preserving the caloric phase transformation. It merges benefits from both homogeneous microstructure and serrated boundary formation.

directions.direction: Surface coating or cladding to mechanically reinforce the bulk while minimally affecting caloric active regions
directions.assessment: While a high-modulus surface coating could increase apparent integrity by retarding crack growth, this approach may risk thermal and field interaction complications that could alter the caloric response. Hence, it is less directly supported.
